say.text: Papillary and follicular carcinoma are the two cancers this module keeps contrasting. Start with papillary.
A pathologist calls a lesion papillary carcinoma. Which feature is the basis of that call?

choices.label: Papillae with fibrovascular cores, seen at low power
Psammoma bodies, the concentric calcifications seen
Optically clear nuclei with grooves and pseudoinclusions
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The name describes the shape of the groups. Ask what the pathologist checks inside each cell at high power.
That choice is not right. Papillae are real, and the name comes from them, so they feel diagnostic.
But papillae are the architecture. The diagnosis rests on something inside the cell, not on the shape of the groups.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one matters: architecture is the easiest feature to see, which is why it misleads.

say.text: That choice is not right. Psammoma bodies are a real papillary feature, so they tempt you as a sign that settles the call.
But they are often present and only supportive. They also occur in serous ovarian tumours, meningioma and mesothelioma.
Right. Papillary carcinoma is diagnosed on its nuclei: optically clear, ground-glass nuclei with grooves and pseudoinclusions.
The papillae are the architecture the name suggests, but the diagnosis rests on the nuclear features.
Now the other side of the contrast. A follicular-pattern nodule has no papillae, and its nuclei look normal. FNAC reports Bethesda IV.
The surgeon wants to know whether it is carcinoma. Which test settles that?

choices.label: Repeat FNAC with a finer needle, more cells
Lobe histology for capsular or vascular invasion
Frozen section of the lobe during surgery
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which tissue shows a whole capsule, and whether the pathologist can see a capsule being crossed on a slide of cells.
That choice is not right. More material feels like a better answer, so a finer needle tempts you.
But follicular lesions look the same on cytology whatever the needle, because invasion is a tissue feature that cytology cannot show.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the key idea: cytology reports the cells, and the diagnosis needs the tissue.

say.text: That choice is not right. A frozen section feels like a quick answer during surgery, so it tempts you.
But frozen section is of little value for follicular lesions, for the same reason: invasion is judged on histology.
Right. Follicular carcinoma is diagnosed only by capsular or vascular invasion, which needs histology. Cytology alone cannot make it.
So the two cancers are called by different tests: papillary on nuclei at FNAC, follicular on invasion at histology.
Another lesion: no papillae at all, but the nuclei are ground-glass with grooves.
Which label does the nuclear picture support?

choices.label: Follicular carcinoma, since there are no papillae
Papillary carcinoma, follicular variant, for its nuclei
Follicular adenoma, since the lesion is encapsulated
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether the papillary label comes from the architecture or from the cell, and then which feature the nuclei are telling you about.
That choice is not right. Missing papillae point you to the follicular pattern, and a follicular pattern feels like a follicular cancer.
But the papillary label is set by the cell. Missing papillae do not rule it out when the nuclei are papillary.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: the follicular variant has the follicular pattern but papillary nuclei.

say.text: That choice is not right. A capsule is what makes many follicular tumours look benign, so it tempts you to call this an adenoma.
But the nuclei decide the family here, and a capsule does not. A follicular-pattern lesion with papillary nuclei is classed with the papillary carcinomas.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember that encapsulation does not settle the label; the nuclei and the invasion do.

say.text: Right. The follicular variant of papillary carcinoma has follicular architecture but papillary nuclei, and it is classed as papillary carcinoma.
Architecture points one way and the nuclei the other. The nuclei decide.
Ignore region and age for a moment. Across a general series of differentiated thyroid cancers, which is the commonest?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about the whole series of thyroid cancers, all ages and all regions, and about share rather than how hard the diagnosis is.
That choice is not right. Follicular carcinoma tempts you because its invasion rules are the ones exam stems love to test.
But how hard a cancer is to diagnose is a separate question from how often it occurs. Check the share in a general series.
Right. Papillary carcinoma is about 80 to 85 per cent of thyroid cancers, which is why it is the commonest overall.
Keep that in mind: the regional question next is about shares, not totals.
Compare two places. In an iodine-sufficient city, papillary carcinoma makes up the larger share of cancers.
In an iodine-deficient hill district, which cancer's share rises relative to the city?

choices.label: Follicular now the commonest cancer in absolute terms
Papillary still commonest, as it is everywhere
Follicular, a larger share than in the city
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Compare proportions, not totals. Ask which cancer's proportion goes up when iodine is scarce.
That choice is not right. The iodine clue tempts you to jump to the top spot, as if the deficiency cancer took over the whole list.
But the question is about a region's share, not the absolute top spot. Read whether the stem asks for totals or proportions.
That is only part of the picture. Papillary carcinoma does stay the commonest overall, but the stem asks what changes with iodine.
Look at what happens to each cancer's share when iodine is scarce.
Right. Iodine-sufficient areas have a higher proportion of papillary carcinoma, while in iodine-deficient areas follicular carcinoma is relatively the most common.
An encapsulated follicular-pattern tumour has papillary-like nuclei and no capsular or vascular invasion.
Which name does current classification give it?

choices.label: Encapsulated follicular variant of papillary carcinoma
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: In this family, what turns a lesion malignant? Then ask whether this lesion has it.
That choice is not right. Papillary-like nuclei tempt you, and older exam keys counted any encapsulated follicular variant as cancer.
But current classification no longer calls the non-invasive form a carcinoma. Check the invasion first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is a key change: the PYQ key and the current name differ here.

say.text: That choice is not right. Minimal invasion sounds like a small cancer, which tempts you when a capsule is present.
But minimal invasion means capsular invasion, and this lesion has none. Without invasion, the label changes.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the word invasion: it is the feature that decides malignancy in this family.

say.text: Right. NIFTP is a non-invasive follicular neoplasm with papillary-like nuclei, reclassified in 2016 as non-malignant.
The invasion check is what separates it from a carcinoma.
A lobectomy specimen: encapsulated, follicular pattern, papillary-like nuclei, and no capsular or vascular invasion.
What is the classification, and what does the patient need next?

choices.label: Encapsulated follicular variant of PTC, so completion surgery
Frozen section fits follicular carcinoma, so total thyroidectomy
NIFTP, not a cancer, so lobectomy alone is enough
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The specimen shows no invasion. Ask what that does to the label, and then what it does to the extent of surgery.
That choice is not right. Papillary-like nuclei and an encapsulated look tempt you towards the older key, which called that pattern cancer.
But without invasion the current classification does not call it a carcinoma, so no completion operation follows from the label alone.
That choice is not right. A frozen section showing a follicular pattern sounds like a quick diagnosis at surgery, so it tempts you.
But frozen section is of little value for follicular lesions, and it cannot show invasion reliably.
Right. Without invasion, the lesion is not a carcinoma, so it does not need a completion operation.
A 40-year-old woman has a solitary nodule. Her TSH is normal, and the ultrasound looks suspicious.
Which test now tells you what the nodule is?

choices.label: Radionuclide scan, to see whether it is hot
Serum thyroglobulin, to check for cancer
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the work-up has already done, and what a scan can tell you about the nodule's function. Then ask which test looks at the nodule's cells.
That choice is not right. A scan feels thorough and quick, so it tempts you as the first step for a nodule.
But a scan sorts function, and it is done only if TSH is low. With a normal TSH it does not answer what the nodule is.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the sequence: TSH, then the scan only if low, and cytology for the nature.

say.text: That choice is not right. Thyroglobulin is a familiar cancer marker, so it tempts you to test for cancer early.
But routine thyroglobulin is not useful for diagnosing a nodule before surgery. It is a follow-up marker once cancer is known.
Right. FNAC is the investigation of choice for the nature of a nodule, once TSH and ultrasound have set the path.
Exam keys once expected FNAC as the first test. Current practice starts with TSH and ultrasound, and FNAC answers the nature.
